extracted.intended_audience: students, journalists, policymakers, and social scientists concerned with public opinion and judgment
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and criteria for evaluating public opinion, common errors of judgment (stereotypes, sampling, time/space misperception, causal inference), and how to form more reliable collective judgments. Applies to commentators, analysts, and policymakers.

rubrics_metrics.name: False absolutism of a stereotype
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid treating abstract principles or stereotypes as eternal truths when discussing concrete affairs; such absolutism censors objections and isolates the issue from context.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Warning that invoking 'eternal principles' when discussing factories, mines, mountains, or political authority turns discussion into fighting; leads to defensive escalation ('buffers for the buffers') and scrambles the affair. Detect by looking for overgeneralized, emotion-driven assertions that exclude contextual facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use contradiction as a clue to stereotyping
rubrics_metrics.description: Contradictions in an argument often indicate that a stereotype is being used to blanket out interfering facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If successive claims about different sectors require mutually incompatible stereotypes, the series of contradictions reveals that the argument was constructed by selecting stereo­types to obliterate inconvenient facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inability to take account of space
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure reasoning accounts for practical geography and distances rather than relying on schematic visual images or inherited strategic stereotypes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: calls to 'reestablish an Eastern Front' ignored the 5,000-mile intervening distance and transport realities. Analysts should consider routes, transport capacity, and logistical feasibility rather than projecting forces 'as on a magic carpet.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish geometrical distance from practical distance
rubrics_metrics.description: Don't equate map distances or straight-line measures with the effective distance to be traversed in practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical distance depends on available transportation, schedules, speeds, costs, and road/sea conditions. Telling someone 'it is three miles' is meaningless unless you specify the mode and quality of travel (walking, motoring, detours, ruts, puddles).

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider practical geography when drawing boundaries
rubrics_metrics.description: Boundary-drawing must reflect on-the-ground realities (factories, streets, villages) rather than abstract ethnic or colored maps.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Warnings about lines drawn by formula (e.g., self-determination) that, when surveyed, cut through buildings or pasture/water resources; planners should survey practical geography to avoid absurd complications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations of imposing permanent rules on the future
rubrics_metrics.description: Be cautious about making rules intended to bind unknown futures (e.g., detailed wills, immutable constitutions); time changes usefulness and circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legal doctrines (e.g., rules against perpetuities) exist because people err in assuming present judgments should rule indefinitely. The amending clause of a constitution signals the drafters' confidence about their opinions' reach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Match time-conception to the thing in hand
rubrics_metrics.description: Decide whether to calculate for the emergency or for the long run; use the time-horizon appropriate to the decision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some problems require decisions based on what will happen in hours, others in years or generations. Wisdom includes distinguishing the proper time-conception; using the wrong time-scale produces errors from dreamer-level neglect of the present to philistine-level neglect of long-term consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize the 'specious present' and ideational present
rubrics_metrics.description: Understand that immediate perception of duration is limited (the 'specious present'); memory and ideation can extend the present by combining perceptions with memory images.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Vividness is proportional to the number of discriminations perceived in the ideational present; activity affects perceived duration vs remembered duration. This affects how people judge events and time-scales.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose time-measure appropriate to practical purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid using astronomical/geological time measures when addressing near-term practical problems and vice versa; the measure chosen should serve the moral/practical purpose of the argument.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: H. G. Wells' scale to visualize 'true proportions' of historical time may be apt for long-term moral perspective, but not for salvaging a civilization reeling from a recent war — the relevant horizon differs by purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid using long-term population replacement as moral justification
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not excuse immediate harm by appealing to long-term demographic recovery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example given: saying millions dying now doesn't matter because birthrates will compensate in two generations is a misuse of a time perspective to justify inertia or cruelty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply proper sustainability calculus for renewable vs nonrenewable resources
rubrics_metrics.description: Resource policy must account for growth rates, reserves, rates of use, economies of use, and select a time-horizon for posterity appropriate to the resource's nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Timber policy should match species' growth and replanting cycles; coal being geologic requires global reserve estimates, projected uses, and a chosen time standard (e.g., 100 years) for what constitutes 'posterity' and how much thrift to demand now.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid locking future generations into obsolete technologies via long monopolies
rubrics_metrics.description: Contracts granting excessively long monopolies (e.g., ninety-nine years) risk condemning posterity to inferior infrastructure if technology changes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer subsidies or shorter-term accommodations rather than long-term concessions when the future of the technology is uncertain; recognize officials often lack a real 'realizing sense' of long durations like ninety-nine years.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be skeptical of 'Historic Rights' based on selectively chosen dates
rubrics_metrics.description: Historical claims depend heavily on the chosen starting date; different dates support different territorial or moral claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In disputes (e.g., Alsace-Lorraine), selections of historical epoch are arbitrary; arguments from history will typically select dates favoring present aims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid essentializing races or nations as eternal types
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that racial or national differences are eternal often ignore historical common origins and change over time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you like a people now you emphasize common ancestry; if you dislike them you stress later divergence. Recognize that such selection of epochs is driven by mood rather than objective truth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware genealogical and gender biases in origin stories
rubrics_metrics.description: Family-tree narratives and genealogies often privilege an invented 'founder' and trace descent preferentially through males.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand that naming a 'founder' is often a convenient choice, not literal Adam-like origin; genealogical tables commonly exhibit male-line bias.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not substitute desired ends for empirical starting points (avoid the 'faith ladder')
rubrics_metrics.description: Resist moving from 'it is fit to be true' to 'it shall be true' by reading future goals back into present facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: William James's faith ladder enumerates steps from possible truth to asserted certainty; while action may help bring about truths, one must avoid mistaking hoped-for ends for present realities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allow necessary time and training for institutional change
rubrics_metrics.description: Policy proposals (e.g., industrial democratization) must sequence responsibility assumption with appropriate training; sudden imposition ignores human learning curves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish functions requiring no training, some training, or lifelong learning; programs should be complementary (responsibility taken in step with training) rather than expecting instantaneous competence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pick fairly a good sample of a large class (statistical sampling standards)
rubrics_metrics.description: When estimating characteristics of large populations, use statistical methods to select representative sample sizes and avoid convenience or access-biased samples.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: for ~200,000 Sheffield workers, Bowley recommended at least 408 men and 408 women (816 total) to limit deviation to 1 in 22. More importantly, select respondents by neutral/accidental/random methods rather than through philanthropists, clubs, or institutions that bias the sample.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid generalizing from convenience or interest-driven samples
rubrics_metrics.description: Casual impressions often rely on samples selected in ways that support preconceptions (e.g., employers judging labor by the most troublesome employee).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that sample selection by contact networks or visible minorities will not represent the whole class; beware assuming organized or vocal subsets reflect the many.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid naive causal inference (post hoc ergo propter hoc)
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not infer cause-and-effect merely from sequence or co-occurrence, especially in complex social phenomena.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Big social issues (business cycles, migrations, diplomatic motives) often have non-obvious causes; trained scholars may disagree after years of study. Hasty intuitive causal linking is unreliable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware emotional association producing false causal links
rubrics_metrics.description: Strong feelings attached to an idea cause unrelated ideas that 'feel' similar to be associated as causes or effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: attributing smallpox to alehouses or connecting Relativity theory to Bolshevism. Emotion 'sucks out' memory corners and entangles otherwise unrelated phenomena; excavation of such emotional reasoning reveals ludicrous entanglements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resist fabricating all-encompassing systems of evil or conspiracy
rubrics_metrics.description: Emotional aggregation of fears leads to systems where everything dreaded is seen as cause or effect of everything else dreaded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such systems arise from accumulation of ancient and recent fears; beware this culminatory tendency when analyzing public fears or political demonization.
